title: Neural Networks and Deep Learning
text:
Prerequisites
Deep learning is the branch of machine learning focused on training neural networks. Neural networks have proven to be powerful across a wide range of domains and tasks, including computer vision, natural language processing, speech recognition, and beyond. The success of these models is partially thanks to the fact that their performance tends to improve as more and more data is used to train them. Further, there have been many advances over the past few decades that have made it easier to attain good performance when using neural networks.
In this course, we will provide a thorough introduction to the field of deep learning. We will cover the basics of building and optimizing neural networks in addition to specifics of different model architectures and training schemes. Beyond the official lecture notes provided here, the course does not follow a specific textbook. Other references (all free) include:
Students should have taken courses on machine learning, linear algebra, and multivariate calculus. Further, it is recommended that students have some basic familiarity with statistical concepts. Finally, students must be proficient in reading and writing Python code. For a list of courses that serve as prerequisites for the undergraduate version of this course, see here.

title: Lecture 1: Introduction, Linear & Logistic Regression
text:
Motivation
Overview. This lecture begins by comparing traditional software, which is generally rule-based; machine learning, which learns patterns and behavior from data; and deep learning, a branch of machine learning that focuses on training neural networks. We then build up to linear models, linear regression and logistic regression, that serve as building blocks for everything else in this course. Specifically, we introduce linear models from the perspective of deep learning in order to present the core concepts of loss functions, gradient descent, and the chain rule for differentiation.

title: Lecture 1: Introduction, Linear & Logistic Regression
text:
Rule-based software
Consider the task of classifying handwritten images as 0 or 1. This task is simple enough that it can mostly be solved with a simple heuristic rule: a 0 almost always has at least two dark pixels crossing its middle row whereas a 1 has just one. This can be hard-coded by hand, producing something like the following:
n_dark = 0
for pixel in middle_row:
    # Assume pixel values range from 0-255
    if pixel < 100:
        n_dark += 1
if n_dark > 1:
    return 0
else:
    return 1
This simple program might work acceptably well for 0 vs 1 classification, but what about classifying all ten handwritten digits? One could start by trying to enumerate different heuristic rules to distinguish the digits, but the wide range of writing styles and possible digit positions and shapes quickly makes a rule-based system intractable. More complex problems–even those that we might consider “simple” like classifying an image as being a picture of a cat or dog–are clearly out of reach.


Machine learning
How can we design computer programs for problems that are too complex to allow for simply writing down a set of rules? In this case, while we might not be able to come up with a rule set, we may be able to come up with a training set, i.e. a collection of inputs and the corresponding desired output for the program.

Definition. Machine learning produces programs whose behavior is learned from data rather than hand-coded. Given examples of desired input–output pairs, machine learning aims to automatically adjust the program to better reproduce the function underlying the input-output mapping.

After collecting a training dataset, the first step in old-fashioned machine learning is to design a set of features. Features are computable measurements about the input (e.g., the number of dark pixels per row or the presence of a certain stroke pattern). We typically represent the input feature values as a feature vector \bm{x} by assembling all feature measurements for a given input into a fixed-length vector. In old-fashioned machine learning, these features are generally used with simple models, i.e. models that are constrained to have a simple structure that makes them amenable to optimization. The use of a simple model makes the success of old-fashioned ML depend heavily on the quality of hand-designed features. Designing the best feature for complex tasks like large-scale object recognition across tens of thousands of categories is challenging, and feature engineering can become the limiting factor in model performance.

Deep learning
What should we do to overcome the limits of feature engineering? Deep learning asks: If we are learning the model, why not learn the features too? In other words, instead of hand-designing features based on intuition and experimentation, perhaps we can directly learn features that are well-suited to the training data. As long as we have sufficient data and can effectively train such models, we might naturally expect this approach to work better. Indeed, since the resurgence of this basic idea in the early 2000s, deep learning has enabled a dizzying array of breakthroughs and transformative technologies.

Definition. Deep learning studies models that are big, complex, differentiable functions built by composing many small, simple, differentiable functions called layers. Because the full composition is differentiable, the parameters of every layer can be trained jointly, end-to-end, with gradient descent.

text:
Why Deep Learning Was Hard
The core techniques underlying deep learning, such as neural networks and gradient descent, have existed since the 1950s. If deep learning is so powerful, why wasn’t it the prevalent approach to machine learning until recently? For old-fashioned ML with fixed features and a simple classifier, the training loss is often convex as a function of the parameters. This means that, under weak assumptions, gradient descent is guaranteed to find the minimum, and we can be reasonably confident that the solution generalizes well to unseen data. In deep learning, we have no such guarantees. In practice, the loss is highly non-convex, and can be riddled with local optima, saddle points, and flat regions. As a result, training itself can be difficult, i.e. the training loss can remain high and hard to bring down, or small errors in training can lead to large errors at test time.

title: Lecture 1: Introduction, Linear & Logistic Regression
text:
Linear Regression
For the rest of this lecture we study two foundational linear models.

Definition. Linear regression is a model that predicts a scalar value from an input feature vector. The prediction is an affine function of the features, meaning that any change in a feature always produces a constant, proportional change in the output.

As a running example, consider the task of predicting a home’s sale price from three features: its age (years), the square footage (sqft), and the number of bedrooms (nbr).
\hat{y} = w_1 \cdot \text{age} + w_2 \cdot \text{sqft} + w_3 \cdot \text{nbr} + b
where w_1, w_2, and w_3 are the weights assigned to each feature value and \hat{y} is the predicted price. The features can be combined into a feature vector \bm{x} = [\text{age},\, \text{sqft},\, \text{nbr}]^\top \in \mathbb{R}^3 and weights into the weight vector \bm{w} = [w_1, w_2, w_3]^\top \in \mathbb{R}^3, giving the standard expression for a linear regression model:
\hat{y} = \bm{w}^\top \bm{x} + b
The weight vector \bm{w} and bias value b are the parameters of the model. Together we write them as the parameter vector \bm{\theta} = (\bm{w}, b). In general, the parameters \bm{\theta} of a given model are the values that are tuned via optimization and “learned” from data.
What if we want to process more than one example at a time? As we will discuss later, this is common during both training and inference, or “test time”, when the trained model is being used to make predictions. We can assemble N feature vectors into a matrix \bm{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}, where d is the feature dimension, and compute the model’s predictions as
\hat{\bm{y}} = \bm{X}\bm{w} + b\bm{1}_N, \qquad \hat{\bm{y}} \in \mathbb{R}^N, \quad \bm{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}, \quad \bm{w} \in \mathbb{R}^d, \quad b \in \mathbb{R}
where \bm{1}_N \in \mathbb{R}^N is the vector of all ones.

The loss function
Given a model, we need a way to tune the parameters to fit the data. To determine how well the model fits the data (and ultimately as an objective to be optimized), we use a loss function. For regression (predicting a scalar value) a common loss function is the squared error loss:
\mathcal{L}(\hat{y}, y) = \frac{1}{2}(\hat{y} - y)^2
where y is the true label for the input \bm{x} used to produce the prediction \hat{y}. The \frac{1}{2} is included for convenience because it will cancel out the exponent of 2 when we differentiate. The goal is to find \bm{\theta} that minimizes \mathcal{L} over the training set.






Note



In the past, you may have fit linear regression via the closed-form solution \bm{w}^* = (\bm{X}^\top \bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^\top \bm{y} that arises when analytically finding the minimum of the loss function. In this course, we ignore the closed-form solution and instead use gradient descent because it generalizes to neural networks whereas a closed-form solution does not. Computing the closed-form solution can also be expensive for large problems because it requires inverting a matrix, while gradient descent can be more computationally efficient.




Gradient descent
Gradient descent is the core optimization algorithm used in deep learning. Gradient descent is an iterative algorithm where, at each step, we move the parameters in the direction that most rapidly decreases the loss. As long as the function being optimized is not too complex and as long as we don’t move too much, we can be confident that we’ve decreased the loss. If we do this over and over again, we might hope to reach a minimum of the function.

Gradient Descent
Initialize parameters \bm{\theta} (we will discuss how to do this later!).
Repeat until a stopping criterion is met: \bm{\theta} \leftarrow \bm{\theta} - \eta\,\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\mathcal{L}
where \eta > 0 is the learning rate and \nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\mathcal{L} is the gradient of the loss with respect to \bm{\theta}.

There are many ways to decide when to stop performing gradient descent. Since loss functions are generally nonnegative, a natural criterion is to wait until the loss reaches zero, but this is only possible if the model can perfectly fit the data. In the case of a linear model, this would mean that the input-output relationship is perfectly linear, which is rarely the case. Other heuristics used as stopping criteria include:

The loss stops decreasing, or its rate of decrease gets sufficiently slow.
Performance on held-out validation data stops improving.
We run out of compute budget or patience.

Apart from the stopping criteria, to use gradient descent we must also specify a learning rate. Broadly, the learning rate dictates how quickly optimization progresses. However, as mentioned above (and as we will discuss further later), the gradient at a given location is only a local property of the function. Too large of a learning rate can therefore prevent gradient descent from making reliable progress and can even cause divergence, where the loss increases. Overall, we strive for a “just right” learning rate where the loss steadily decreases.

Gradient Descent Explorer

  label: "Learning rate η"})
viewof gdW0 = Inputs.range([-3, 3], {step: 0.1, value: 2.5,
  label: "Initial value w₀"})
viewof gdNSteps = Inputs.range([1, 30], {step: 1, value: 12,
  label: "Steps"})

gdGrad = w => w - 1

  let traj = []
  let w = gdW0
  for (let i = 0; i <= gdNSteps; i++) {
    traj.push({step: i, w, loss: gdLoss(w)})
    w = w - gdEta * gdGrad(w)
  }
  return traj
}

Computing the gradients: the chain rule
Performing gradient descent requires \nabla_{\bm{\theta}} \mathcal{L}, or in the case of linear regression, \nabla_{\bm{w}}\mathcal{L} and \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial b}. For a differentiable model, we can compute these conveniently by applying the chain rule, which treats \mathcal{L} as a composition of functions.
For example, when computing the loss of a single training example (\bm{x}, y) using linear regression, we have
\hat{y} = \bm{w}^\top \bm{x} + b, \qquad \mathcal{L} = \tfrac{1}{2}(\hat{y} - y)^2
If we consider \mathcal{L} as a function of \hat{y} and \hat{y} as a function of \bm{w} (or b) and apply the chain rule, we have
\frac{d\mathcal{L}}{d\bm{w}} = \frac{d\mathcal{L}}{d\hat{y}} \cdot \frac{d\hat{y}}{d\bm{w}}, \qquad \frac{d\mathcal{L}}{db} = \frac{d\mathcal{L}}{d\hat{y}} \cdot \frac{d\hat{y}}{db}
We can compute these derivatives individually as  \dfrac{d\mathcal{L}}{d\hat{y}} = \hat{y} - y, \qquad \dfrac{d\hat{y}}{d\bm{w}} = \bm{x}, \qquad \dfrac{d\hat{y}}{db} = 1
Substituting in these individual derivatives, we have
\nabla_{\bm{w}}\mathcal{L} = (\hat{y} - y)\,\bm{x}, \qquad \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial b} = \hat{y} - y
For linear regression, the gradient has a clean interpretation: the update for weight w_i is the prediction error (\hat{y} - y) scaled by the feature value x_i. In this way, features that appear more strongly in the input receive proportionally larger weight updates.


Mini-batch stochastic gradient descent
So far, we have computed the gradient of the loss for a single example. In practice it is common to compute the gradient for more than one example and update the parameters using the average gradient, like so:
\bm{\theta} \leftarrow \bm{\theta} - \frac{\eta}{B} \sum_{i=1}^{B} \nabla_{\bm{\theta}} \mathcal{L}^{(i)}
where B is called the batch size. In the most extreme case, we could set the batch size equal to our training set size and compute the average gradient of all of the examples in our training set. However, computing the gradient for every example at every step of training might be unnecessarily expensive, as we will discuss later. More common in deep learning is therefore to draw a random sample of B examples from the training set at each iteration.


Hyperparameters
Unlike parameters like \bm{w} and b, hyperparameters are generally not learned from data but instead are set by the practitioner, typically through trial and error or heuristics. So far we have observed the following hyperparameters:



Hyperparameter
Description




\eta (learning rate)
Step size per gradient update


Batch size B
Number of examples per gradient update


Stopping criterion
When to stop training


Initialization scheme
Starting values for \bm{w} and b



We will revisit all of these as the course progresses.

title: Lecture 1: Introduction, Linear & Logistic Regression
text:
Softmax (Logistic) Regression
The goal of regression is to produce a continuous scalar value. However, many problems of interest involve assigning the input a discrete label from a set of possible class labels. Such problems are referred to classification tasks.
Labels are further distinguished by the fact that, unlike the continuous values predicted during regression, they generally are unordered. For example, there is a natural order to the value of a house because a price of $213,000 is more than $190,000. In contrast, if we are predicting whether an image contains a picture of a cat or a dog, it would not be valid to say “cat is greater than dog” (or vice versa).
To turn our running “home price prediction” example into a classification task, we could instead aim to predict whether a given home would sell above asking, below asking, or not sell. In this way, it becomes a 3-class classification problem. As before, we will aim to make this prediction from its age, square footage, number of bedrooms, and asking price.

One-hot encoding
Representing class labels as integer class IDs (e.g. 1, 2, 3) would imply some kind of ordering. We instead represent class labels as one-hot vectors, which are length-K (where K is the number of classes) vectors with a 1 at the position of the correct class and 0s elsewhere. In the home price example, we would use the following three one-hot vectors for our classes:

\begin{aligned}
\text{“below asking”} &\;\to\; \bm{y} = [1,\, 0,\, 0]^\top \\
\text{“above asking”} &\;\to\; \bm{y} = [0,\, 1,\, 0]^\top \\
\text{“not sold”} &\;\to\; \bm{y} = [0,\, 0,\, 1]^\top
\end{aligned}

Note that the (Euclidean) distance between any two distinct one-hot vectors is always \sqrt{2}, thereby implying no order of any kind. As we will see later, one-hot vectors can also be interpreted as a probability distribution, where a given example’s assigned class is given a probability of 1 and the remaining classes have probability 0.


From scores to probabilities
To make a prediction, a softmax regression model first computes a score o_j for each class via a linear transformation of the features:
\bm{o} = \bm{W}\bm{x} + \bm{b}, \qquad \bm{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times d},\;\; \bm{b} \in \mathbb{R}^K,\;\; \bm{o} \in \mathbb{R}^K
For the running example (K=3, d=4), \bm{W} has 3 \times 4 = 12 entries and \bm{b} has 3, so the model has 15 parameters in all. A larger score means the model considers that class more likely. Note that each of these scores are produced in essentially the same way as the scalar output of a linear regression model. To convert the set of predicted scores to a valid probability distribution (non-negative, summing to 1), we apply the softmax function:
\operatorname{softmax}(\bm{o})_j = \frac{\exp(o_j)}{\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{K} \exp(o_k)}
Since \exp(o_j) \geq 0 for all j, the output values of softmax are non-negative. Additionally, we have that
\sum_j \operatorname{softmax}(\bm{o})_j = \frac{\displaystyle \sum_{j = 1}^K \exp(o_j)}{\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{K} \exp(o_k)} = 1
Consequently, the output of the softmax function forms a valid probability distribution. We therefore can write the full softmax regression model as
P(y \mid \bm{x}) = \operatorname{softmax}(\bm{W}\bm{x} + \bm{b})
Effectively, as a given class’ score becomes higher, the model assigns a higher probability to that class and a lower probability to the other classes.

Softmax Explorer

viewof smO1 = Inputs.range([-5, 5], {step: 0.1, value: 2.0, label: "Score o₁ (below asking)"})

  const exps = scores.map(o => Math.exp(o - m))
  const s = exps.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0)
  return exps.map(e => e / s)
}

title: Lecture 1: Introduction, Linear & Logistic Regression
text:
Cross-Entropy Loss
For linear regression, we used a squared error loss. While it is technically possible to use a squared error loss to train a softmax regression model, in practice it is much more common to use the cross-entropy loss.1

From maximum likelihood to cross-entropy
Recall that we can consider softmax regression as producing a probability distribution over classes conditioned on the input. A natural objective would therefore be to maximize the probability the model assigns to the true class, computed on a dataset of labeled examples. Concretely, given N training examples \{(\bm{x}^{(i)}, \bm{y}^{(i)})\}_{i=1}^N, we can start by aiming to maximize the joint likelihood:
\max_{\bm{\theta}} \prod_{i=1}^{N} P_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{y}^{(i)} \mid \bm{x}^{(i)})
It’s typical to maximize the log likelihood instead, because the logarithm is a monotonic function (so the parameter values corresponding to the maximum don’t change when you apply it) and because a product of probabilities can cause underflow and other numerical instabilities. Additionally, in machine learning we generally minimize a loss rather than maximize an objective. This leads to the minimization of the negative log-likelihood:
\min_{\bm{\theta}} -\sum_{i=1}^{N} \log P_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{y}^{(i)} \mid \bm{x}^{(i)})
We can write this in the following equivalent form:
\min_{\bm{\theta}} -\sum_{i=1}^{N} \sum_{j=1}^{K} \bm{y}_j^{(i)} \log P_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{y}_j^{(i)} \mid \bm{x}^{(i)})
by noting that \bm{y}^{(i)} is one-hot. This final equation is the cross-entropy loss, a quantity from information theory that measures how “wrong” a probability distribution is relative to the ground truth.
We can express the cross-entropy loss for a single example using the softmax regression model with scores \bm{o} = \bm{W}\bm{x} + \bm{b} and one-hot label \bm{y} as

\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{L}(\bm{y}, \hat{\bm{y}}) &= -\sum_j y_j \log \frac{\exp(o_j)}{\sum_k \exp(o_k)} \\
&= \sum_j y_j \log \sum_k \exp(o_k) - \sum_j y_j o_j \\
&= \log \sum_k \exp(o_k) \;-\; \sum_j y_j o_j
\end{aligned}

where the simplifications come from the quotient rule of the logarithm and the fact that \sum_j y_j = 1. To perform gradient descent, we only need one additional term compared to those used in linear regression: \frac{d\mathcal{L}}{do_j}. The reexpression above makes \frac{d\mathcal{L}}{do_j} straightforward to derive:

\begin{aligned}
\frac{d\mathcal{L}}{do_j} &= \frac{d}{do_j}\!\left[\log \sum_k \exp(o_k)\right] - y_j \\
& = \frac{\exp(o_j)}{\sum_k \exp(o_k)} - y_j \\
&= \operatorname{softmax}(\bm{o})_j - y_j \\
&= \hat{y}_j - y_j
\end{aligned}

which can be expressed in vector form as \nabla_{\bm{o}} \mathcal{L} = \hat{\bm{y}} - \bm{y}. Intuitively, the gradient of the cross-entropy loss for the softmax regression model is simply the gap between the predicted probability and the ground-truth label. When the model assigns all of its probability to the correct label, the gradient is zero; but as the model becomes more incorrect, the gradient increases.

text:
Limitations of Linear Models
Recap. Recall from Lecture 1 that both linear regression and logistic regression are considered linear models1. In this lecture, we study: What does it mean for a model to be linear, precisely? What are the limitations of linear models? What kinds of relationships can they not capture? How can we overcome these limitations, and how do we train the resulting model?
More precisely, a linear model satisfies two properties, one of which subsumes the other:
crumbs: 3  Lecture 2: Multi-Layer Perceptrons & Backpropagation

title: Lecture 2: Multi-Layer Perceptrons & Backpropagation
text:
Definition. A model \hat{y} = wx + b is a linear model2 if an increase or decrease in any feature must always increase or decrease the output, respectively, by the same proportional amount, regardless of the current value of x.



Monotonicity (necessary, but not sufficient). If w > 0, then x \uparrow \Rightarrow \hat{y} \uparrow always (and vice versa for w < 0); the direction never flips. Every linear model is monotonic — but the converse fails. An exponential relationship, for instance, is monotonic (it never reverses direction) yet is not linear, since it grows faster and faster rather than at a constant rate.
Constant effect (necessary and sufficient). The rate of change \dfrac{\partial\hat{y}}{\partial x} = w is the same everywhere, regardless of the current value of x. Graphically, \hat{y} vs x is a straight line. This alone fully characterizes linearity — and it forces monotonicity as a side effect.


When linearity fails
Some relationships are approximately linear. For instance, larger houses tend to cost more, and a straight line is a reasonable first approximation. Others are monotonic but not linear: transistor counts on computer chips have grown every decade (property 1), but the growth accelerates rather than proceeding at a constant rate (property 2 fails) — an exponential curve, not a straight line. And some relationships are neither: consider doctor visits vs. age: visits are very frequent in infancy, drop through young adulthood, then climb again in old age. This U-shaped curve is neither monotonic nor linear.






Linear: As house size increases, price rises monotonically when other factors remain unchanged; a linear model captures this perfectly.







Monotonic, not linear: transistor counts have grown every decade (property 1 holds) but at an accelerating, not constant, rate (property 2 fails) — no straight line fits this curve.







Neither: doctor visits follow a U-shaped curve over age; no linear model can represent this.





A classic ML solution is hand-engineering: since exponential relationships like the transistor count example above are monotonic but not linear, statisticians take \log x to linearize them before fitting a linear model. In deep learning we reject that. We learn the features automatically.

text:
The Multi-Layer Perceptron
Remember, the central idea in deep learning is to build complex models that can model complex relationships by composing many simple, differentiable functions.

Why stacking linear layers doesn’t help
We have already seen one example of a layer in this class: The linear layer underlying linear and logistic regression. Given that we’ve already been exposed to linear layers, let’s try composing two of them:
H = XW_1, \qquad O = HW_2
Substituting: by associativity, O = (XW_1)W_2 = X(W_1W_2) =: XW — a product of matrices is itself just a matrix, so this has the same form as a single linear layer.






Warning



Key fact. Composing any number of linear (affine) layers always collapses to a single linear (affine) map. Depth adds no expressive power without nonlinearity.




Adding nonlinearity
The fix: insert a nonlinear function \sigma (the activation function or nonlinearity) between the linear layers:
\boxed{H = \sigma(XW_1 + b_1), \qquad O = HW_2 + b_2}
Because \sigma is nonlinear, O is now a nonlinear function of X.
Element-wise application. Inside neural networks \sigma is applied element-wise:
h_i = \sigma(x_i)
Each output element depends on exactly one input element (\sigma is a scalar function of a scalar) replicated independently at every position. This is in contrast to softmax (from Lecture 1), where every output depends on all inputs.


Architecture and Terminology


  
  
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
  
  
  
    
    
    
    
  
  
  
    
  
  
    x₁x₂x₃
  
  
  
    
    
  
  
    h₁h₂
    h₃h₄
  
  
  
    
  
  
    o₁o₂
  
  
  
    Input x ∈ ℝ³
    H = σ(XW₁+b₁)
    O = HW₂+b₂
  
  
  
    Layer 0
    Layer 1 (hidden)
    Layer 2 (output)
  
  
  
  W₁, b₁ then σ
  
  W₂, b₂


The architecture above is a two-layer (by convention, counting weight layers — not the input Layer 0) fully-connected multi-layer perceptron (MLP). Every input is connected to every hidden unit, and every hidden unit to every output, hence fully connected. The names for this architecture:







Name
Notes




Multi-layer perceptron (MLP)
Historical; from the Perceptron (Rosenblatt 1958)

Preferred modern term

Emphasises all-to-all connectivity

Common in Keras / TensorFlow

title: Lecture 2: Multi-Layer Perceptrons & Backpropagation
text:
Backpropagation
Let \mathcal{L} denote the loss function, a scalar that measures the discrepancy between the model’s predictions and the true targets. Training proceeds by minimizing \mathcal{L} using gradient descent, which requires computing the gradient of the loss with respect to every parameter in the model, i.e., \dfrac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W^m} for each weight matrix W^m.
Backpropagation provides an algorithm for evaluating all such gradients by systematically applying the chain rule of calculus from the output layer back to the input layer. It can achieve more efficiency by reusing intermediate quantities computed during the forward pass, avoiding redundant calculations and enabling gradient computation in time proportional to a single forward evaluation.

The Chain Rule — Two Cases
Case 1: single intermediate variable. If \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}(z(w)):
\frac{d\mathcal{L}}{dw} = \frac{d\mathcal{L}}{dz}\,\frac{dz}{dw}
Case 2: multiple intermediate variables. If \mathcal{L} reaches w through z_1(w), z_2(w), \ldots, z_N(w) independently, i.e. \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}(z_1(w), z_2(w), \ldots, z_N(w)):
\frac{d\mathcal{L}}{dw} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial z_i}\,\frac{dz_i}{dw}
Think of it as: sum the derivative contribution along every path from w to \mathcal{L}. Both cases come up repeatedly in the backprop derivation.


Notation and Definitions
For an L-layer MLP:








Symbol
Meaning
Shape




L
Number of layers
scalar (integer)


N^m
Width (# units) of layer m
scalar (integer)


W^m
Weight matrix for layer m
\mathbb{R}^{N^m \times N^{m-1}}


b^m
Bias vector for layer m
\mathbb{R}^{N^m}


\sigma^m
Nonlinearity at layer m
\mathbb{R}^{N^m} \to \mathbb{R}^{N^m} (element-wise)


a^m
Pre-activations for layer m
\mathbb{R}^{N^m}


h^m
Activations for layer m
\mathbb{R}^{N^m}


h^0
Model input \mathbf{x}
\mathbb{R}^{N^0}


y
Target output
\mathbb{R}^{N^L}


\mathcal{L}
Loss: \mathcal{L}(h^L,\, y) \in \mathbb{R}
scalar (real number)



The forward pass computes, for m = 1, \ldots, L:
a^m = W^m h^{m-1} + b^m \qquad (\text{pre-activations}) h^m = \sigma^m(a^m) \qquad (\text{activations})
Backprop requires two quantities pre-specified from the model design:

\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial h^L}: derivative of the loss w.r.t. the model output (e.g. cross-entropy gradient).
\frac{dh^m}{da^m} = (\sigma^m)'(a^m): derivative of the nonlinearity (sigmoid, ReLU, etc.), computed in Activation Functions.



Deriving the Weight Gradient
We want \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W^m_{ij}} for any entry (i,j), where i \in \{1,\ldots,N^m\} indexes the unit in layer m (row) and j \in \{1,\ldots,N^{m-1}\} indexes the unit in layer m-1 (column). In other words, W^m_{ij} is the weight of the connection from unit j in layer m-1 to unit i in layer m.
Step 1 — Apply the chain rule, pivoting through a^m.
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W^m_{ij}} = \sum_{k=1}^{N^m} \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^m_k} \frac{\partial a^m_k}{\partial W^m_{ij}}
Step 2 — Evaluate \partial a^m_k / \partial W^m_{ij}.
Expanding a^m_k explicitly: a^m_k = \sum_{\ell=1}^{N^{m-1}} W^m_{k\ell}\,h^{m-1}_\ell + b^m_k.
The weight W^m_{ij} appears only in the formula for a^m_i (the i-th row). Therefore:
\frac{\partial a^m_k}{\partial W^m_{ij}} = \begin{cases} h^{m-1}_j & k = i \\ 0 & k \neq i \end{cases}
Step 3 — Collapse the sum. All terms except k=i are zero:
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W^m_{ij}} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^m_i} \cdot h^{m-1}_j
Step 4 — Matrix form. The vector \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^m} has shape N^m and h^{m-1} has shape N^{m-1}. Their outer product gives the gradient matrix of shape N^m \times N^{m-1}, matching W^m:

\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W^m} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^m} \cdot (h^{m-1})^\top

The bias gradient follows the same derivation and is simpler: differentiating a^m_i with respect to b^m_i gives 1 rather than h^{m-1}_j, so \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial b^m} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^m}.


The Backward Recursion
We still need \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^m}. This is where the “back” in backprop comes from.
Base case (m = L):
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^L} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial h^L} \odot \frac{dh^L}{da^L}
Both factors are pre-specified. \odot is element-wise (Hadamard) multiplication.
Recursive case (m < L): Expanding via the chain rule, pivoting through the next layer’s pre-activations a^{m+1}:
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^m_k} = \left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{N^{m+1}} \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^{m+1}_\ell} \cdot W^{m+1}_{\ell k}\right) \cdot \frac{dh^m_k}{da^m_k}
In matrix form:

\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^m} = \left({W^{m+1}}^\top \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^{m+1}}\right) \odot \frac{dh^m}{da^m}

The key observation: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^m} depends on \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^{m+1}}; the gradient one layer forward. Starting from m=L and going backwards, each step feeds the next. This is backpropagation.
Summarized as a clean algorithm:

Backpropagation Algorithm
Pre-specify (from model design):

\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial h^L} — loss gradient w.r.t. the model output.
\frac{dh^m}{da^m} = (\sigma^m)'(a^m) — nonlinearity derivative at each layer.

Forward pass — compute and cache all activations: h^0 = \mathbf{x}, \quad a^m = W^m h^{m-1} + b^m, \quad h^m = \sigma^m(a^m), \quad m=1,\ldots,L
Step 1 — Base case (output layer): \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^L} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial h^L} \odot \frac{dh^L}{da^L}
Step 2 — Backward recursion for m = L-1, L-2, \ldots, 1: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^m} = \underbrace{\left({W^{m+1}}^\top \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^{m+1}}\right)}_{\text{from prev step}} \odot \underbrace{\frac{dh^m}{da^m}}_{\text{known}}
Step 3 — Weight gradients for all m: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W^m} = \underbrace{\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^m}}_{\text{step 2}} \cdot \underbrace{(h^{m-1})^\top}_{\text{forward pass}}
Gradient descent update: W^m \leftarrow W^m - \eta\,\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W^m}

Why is this efficient? A single forward pass (caching all a^m) plus a single backward pass gives all weight gradients simultaneously. Without caching, computing the gradient for layer 1 would require recomputing the same intermediate quantities over and over — far more expensive work that caching avoids at the cost of a little memory.


Connecting Back to Vanishing Gradients
In the backward recursion, each step multiplies by \frac{dh^m}{da^m}. For sigmoid, \max_x \frac{d}{dx}\operatorname{sigmoid}(x) = \frac{1}{4}. In an L-layer sigmoid network, the gradient reaching layer 1 is scaled by roughly \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^L, vanishing rapidly. For ReLU, the derivative in the active region is exactly 1 (no shrinkage). Toggle the “Tanh/Sigmoid + overlay derivatives” in the explorer above to see the saturation visually.

title: Lecture 2: Multi-Layer Perceptrons & Backpropagation
text:
Summary






Note



Key takeaways from Lecture 2

Linear models cannot represent nonlinear relationships. Stacking affine layers collapses to a single affine map; depth buys nothing without nonlinearity.
Nonlinearity (an element-wise activation function \sigma) injected between linear layers gives the MLP its expressive power.
Sigmoid was the historical default; it suffers from vanishing gradients due to saturating derivatives. ReLU (gradient = 1 for x>0) avoids this and dominates modern practice.
Backpropagation is a three-step algorithm: (1) base case at the output layer, (2) backward recursion using the weight transpose, (3) outer product to get weight gradients. The forward pass caches activations to avoid recomputation.
The Universal Approximation Theorem guarantees a wide enough single-hidden-layer MLP can approximate any continuous function on a bounded domain to arbitrary accuracy, but overfitting, model size, and the question of how to train are all open challenges.



Next lecture: Regularization and Overfitting - how to prevent the MLP from simply memorizing training data?

The predicted probability \hat y=\operatorname{sigmoid}(wx+b) is not itself linear — or even affine — in x: its rate of change \partial\hat y/\partial x = w\,\hat y(1-\hat y) varies with x, as Activation Functions shows. Logistic regression is a generalized linear model: linear in the parameters, with a fixed nonlinear link function (sigmoid) mapping scores to probabilities — unlike the learned, stacked nonlinearities in an MLP.↩︎
Strictly speaking wx+b is affine, not linear (f(0)=b\neq0 unless b=0) — a true linear function satisfies f(cx)=cf(x). “Linear model” is standard ML/DL shorthand for the affine form (Goodfellow et al. 2016) (see Chapter 5 “Machine Learning Basics”, p. 107, §5.1.4 “Example: Linear Regression”).↩︎

text:
Backpropagation, Continued
Recap. In Lecture 2, we derived backpropagation: a base case at the output layer, a backward recursion through the weight transpose, and an outer product to recover weight gradients. In this lecture, we ask what backprop costs, work through a full example that reveals why gradients can vanish or explode, use that insight to derive a principled way to initialize parameters, see how automatic differentiation turns backprop into a mechanical procedure a computer can run for us, and finally, turn to overfitting: why models memorize training data, and the two regularizers (i.e., weight decay and dropout) used to stop them.

title: Lecture 3: Under/overfitting, Regularization, Numerical Stability, Autodiff
text:
Recap: The Three Steps
Recall from Backpropagation the three ingredients of backpropagation, for an L-layer model with pre-activations a^m, activations h^m = \sigma^m(a^m), and loss \mathcal{L}:

\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^L} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial h^L} \odot \frac{dh^L}{da^L} \qquad\text{(base case)} \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^m} = \left({W^{m+1}}^\top \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^{m+1}}\right) \odot \frac{dh^m}{da^m} \qquad\text{(recursion, } m = L-1, \ldots, 1\text{)} \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W^m} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^m} \cdot (h^{m-1})^\top \qquad\text{(weight gradient)}



The Cost of Backpropagation
Suppose the model is a stack of matrix multiplies and element-wise nonlinearities. Which is more expensive: a matrix multiply, or an element-wise nonlinearity? The matrix multiply. It does one multiply-add per entry of the weight matrix, and a weight matrix has far more entries than the layer has units. So the cost of a layer is dominated by its matrix multiply, and the forward pass costs roughly one multiply per parameter, summed over all layers: O(|\theta|), where |\theta| is the total number of parameters.
Now, look at the backward recursion above. It also does a matrix–vector product with W^{m+1} at every layer, which has the same asymptotic cost as the forward pass. The weight-gradient step is an outer product that produces an object as large as W^m itself, again with the same cost. So:








Pass
What it computes
Cost




Forward
a^m, h^m for all m
\sim |\theta|


Backward: recursion
\partial \mathcal{L}/\partial a^m for all m
\sim |\theta|


Backward: weight grads
\partial \mathcal{L}/\partial W^m for all m
\sim |\theta|









Note



Rule of thumb. One training step (forward + backward) costs about three forward passes: \sim 3|\theta|. This is why people often estimate training compute directly from parameter count.




Worked Example: A Sigmoid Network
To see why initialization matters, let’s push the recursion through a concrete network: sigmoid activations at every layer, including the output (h^m = \operatorname{sigmoid}(a^m) for all m, including m=L), trained with the binary cross-entropy loss:
\mathcal{L}(y, h^L) = (y-1)\log(1-h^L) - y\log(h^L)
Base case. Applying the chain rule, \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^L} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial h^L}\frac{dh^L}{da^L}, where the first factor is the cross-entropy derivative and the second is the sigmoid derivative:
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^L} = \underbrace{\frac{h^L - y}{h^L(1-h^L)}}_{\text{cross-entropy}} \cdot \underbrace{h^L(1-h^L)}_{\text{sigmoid}'} \;=\; h^L - y
The h^L(1-h^L) terms cancel exactly, leaving the same remarkably clean result we saw for softmax in Cross-Entropy Loss: the gradient is simply the prediction error.
One step of the recursion. Substituting into the backward recursion:
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^{L-1}} = \left({W^L}^\top (h^L - y)\right) \odot h^{L-1}(1-h^{L-1})
and the corresponding weight gradient is \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W^{L-1}} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^{L-1}} \cdot (h^{L-2})^\top. Every further step of the recursion just multiplies in one more weight matrix transpose and one more sigmoid-derivative factor. After many layers, \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^m} is a product of many (W^{k})^\top terms and many sigmoid-derivative terms, chained together.

title: Lecture 3: Under/overfitting, Regularization, Numerical Stability, Autodiff
text:
Vanishing and Exploding Gradients
Two repeated multiplications drive the recursion, and each can misbehave:


  
    
      
    
  

  
  sigmoid(x)
  
  
  x
  sigmoid(x)
  
  
  0
  
  0.5
  
  1
  
  
  
  
  0

  
  
  1/2

  
  d/dx sigmoid(x)
  
  
  x
  d/dx sigmoid(x)
  
  
  0
  
  0.25
  
  
  
  
  0

  
  
  1/4


The nonlinearity term. The sigmoid’s derivative is at most \tfrac14 (at x=0) and is otherwise smaller. Multiplying numbers between 0 and \tfrac14 together, over and over, drives the product toward 0 exponentially fast in the number of layers. Since this factor appears once per layer in the recursion, the gradient reaching the early layers of a deep sigmoid network is scaled by roughly (\tfrac14)^L and it vanishes. And if \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W^m} \approx 0, the gradient-descent update W^m \leftarrow W^m - \eta \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W^m} barely changes W^m at all. The early layers simply stop learning.






Warning



This is why sigmoid is rarely used as a hidden-layer activation. ReLU’s derivative is exactly 0 or exactly 1. Multiplying by 1 repeatedly neither shrinks nor grows the gradient. This is one of the reasons ReLU made training much deeper networks practical.


The weight-matrix term. The recursion also repeatedly multiplies by (W^{k})^\top. What happens when you multiply a matrix by itself over and over depends on its eigenvalues: values consistently above 1 tend to blow the product up (exploding gradients); values consistently below 1 tend to shrink it to zero (vanishing again). The recursion uses a different matrix at each layer, so what matters is how much each one tends to stretch or shrink vectors, but the idea is the same. Unlike the nonlinearity term, this direction of failure is entirely in our hands. It’s set by how we choose the weight matrices before training even starts.

title: Lecture 3: Under/overfitting, Regularization, Numerical Stability, Autodiff
text:
Parameter Initialization
Gradient descent only ever nudges parameters by a small step in the direction of the negative gradient — the initial values are the one place we have direct control, before training dynamics take over. So we should choose that starting distribution carefully.
Two bad ideas, first. Why not initialize every weight to 0? Then every layer’s output stops depending on the input entirely (ignoring the bias), and the model can’t represent any input–output mapping. Training can’t easily fix this either: the backward recursion multiplies by {W^{m+1}}^\top = 0, so at initialization every layer below the output receives exactly zero gradient, and even once updates begin, every unit within a layer stays identical. Why not make every weight the same constant, say 1? Then every row of W computes the same dot product with the input, so every hidden unit learns an identical, totally redundant function — we waste nearly all of the layer’s capacity. We need random, but carefully-scaled, initial values.

Deriving Xavier / Glorot Initialization
Consider one linear layer in isolation, \bm{o} = W\bm{x}, with \bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{in}} and \bm{o}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{out}}. Assume no nonlinearity, x_j \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1), and W_{ij} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2) — the only knob we control is \sigma.
Since o_i = \sum_{j=1}^{n_{in}} W_{ij}\, x_j is a sum of zero-mean terms, \mathbb{E}[o_i] = 0. For the variance, using \mathrm{Var}[o_i] = \mathbb{E}[o_i^2] - \mathbb{E}[o_i]^2 = \mathbb{E}[o_i^2] and independence of all the W_{ij} and x_j (so every cross term W_{ij}W_{ik}x_jx_k with j \neq k has zero mean):
\mathrm{Var}[o_i] = \sum_{j=1}^{n_{in}} \mathbb{E}[W_{ij}^2]\,\mathbb{E}[x_j^2] = \sum_{j=1}^{n_{in}} \sigma^2 \cdot 1 = n_{in}\,\sigma^2
Forward pass. If we want activations to keep the same scale layer after layer (variance \approx 1, matching the input), we need n_{in}\sigma^2 = 1.
Backward pass. The same argument applied to the backward recursion (which multiplies by W^\top instead of W) requires n_{out}\sigma^2 = 1 to keep gradient variance stable.
We can’t satisfy both exactly unless n_{in} = n_{out}, so we average the two constraints as a compromise: \frac{n_{in}\sigma^2 + n_{out}\sigma^2}{2} = 1, giving:

\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{2}{n_{in} + n_{out}}}

This is Xavier (or Glorot) initialization (Glorot and Bengio 2010) — sample every weight from \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2) with this \sigma. Because the activation variance stays \approx 1 at every layer, neither the forward activations nor the backward gradients can systematically explode or vanish.






Note



He initialization. Xavier’s derivation assumes no nonlinearity. If you instead assume a ReLU activation (as Homework 3 does), the same style of derivation gives a slightly different scale, \sigma = \sqrt{2/n_{in}}, called He initialization (He et al. 2015). Most deep learning frameworks default to one of these two schemes.

text:
Automatic Differentiation
So far, every gradient in this course was derived by hand: we wrote down the chain rule for a specific loss and a specific set of layers. Automatic differentiation (autodiff, or autograd) turns this into a mechanical procedure that a computer performs for any composition of functions you define — it is what powers every modern deep learning framework (PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX, …) under the hood.
The trick is to decompose computation into elementary operations (add, multiply, subtract, raise-to-a-power, ReLU, …) simple enough that we can write down each one’s derivative once, in general, and never think about it again.

A Worked Example
Take a tiny scalar network: a hidden unit h = \operatorname{ReLU}(w_h x + b_h), an output o = w_o h + b_o, and squared error loss \mathcal{L} = (y - o)^2. To automatically differentiate, break every line into one elementary operation at a time:
m_h = w_h \cdot x \qquad a_h = m_h + b_h \qquad h = \operatorname{ReLU}(a_h) m_o = w_o \cdot h \qquad o = m_o + b_o \qquad e = y - o \qquad \mathcal{L} = e^2
Each line is one op: multiply, add, ReLU, multiply, add, subtract, power. This is about as far as we can decompose things — and there are only a few dozen such ops in total, shared and reused everywhere.

The diagram above is the computational graph: a directed acyclic graph where each circle is either an operation node (computed from its inputs) or a leaf node (an input or a parameter — the things we might want a derivative with respect to). To compute \frac{d\mathcal{L}}{dw_h}, we find the path in the graph from \mathcal{L} down to w_h, and multiply the local derivative at every operation node along the way:
\frac{d\mathcal{L}}{dw_h} = \frac{d\mathcal{L}}{de}\cdot\frac{de}{do}\cdot\frac{do}{dm_o}\cdot\frac{dm_o}{dh}\cdot\frac{dh}{da_h}\cdot\frac{da_h}{dm_h}\cdot\frac{dm_h}{dw_h}
Every factor here is the derivative of a single, simple operation — exactly the kind of thing we can hard-code once per op and never re-derive. (If a node has more than one path to \mathcal{L}, sum the contributions of each path — this is exactly the “multiple intermediate variables” case of the chain rule from Backpropagation.)

Automatic Differentiation
Define, once, for a small library of elementary ops (add, multiply, subtract, power, ReLU, …):

forward: how to compute the op’s output from its inputs.
backward: the derivative of the op’s output with respect to each input.

Given a user’s model (a composition of these ops):

Forward pass — evaluate every op in order, and record which ops were applied to which inputs. This record is the computational graph.
Backward pass — starting from d\mathcal{L}/d\mathcal{L} = 1, visit the nodes in reverse topological order (each node only after every node that uses it). At each op node, multiply the node’s accumulated gradient by the op’s derivative with respect to each input, and add the result to that input’s running gradient. When the sweep finishes, every leaf w holds d\mathcal{L}/dw. Accumulating into a running sum is how the “sum over paths” is computed without enumerating paths, and one sweep yields the gradients for all leaves at once.


This is exactly what Homework 3 asks you to build: an Operation class (with Add, Mul, ReLU, MatMul, … subclasses) that knows its own forward and backward rules, a Node class that records which operation and parents produced each value, and a backward() that walks the graph to produce every gradient automatically — no more hand-deriving a custom backward pass per architecture.

text:
Overfitting and Regularization
Recall the Universal Approximation Theorem (Universal Approximation Theorem): a sufficiently wide network can fit any function, including simply memorizing a finite training set. So overfitting is a real risk, and it isn’t specific to neural networks at all; the same ideas apply to any sufficiently flexible model.


  
    
      
    
  

  
  Overfitting
  
  
  iteration

The classic symptom (left) is a gap that opens up between training and validation loss: training loss keeps falling while validation loss bottoms out and starts rising. The classic picture of why (right): given noisy samples of some true function, a good fit stays close to the true curve everywhere, while an overfit model contorts itself to pass exactly through every training point — at the cost of wild, high-error excursions everywhere else.

How Can a Linear Model Overfit?
It’s tempting to think a model as simple as \hat{y} = \bm{w}^\top\bm{x} can’t overfit. But consider: for an example with label y \in \{-1, +1\}, each feature is sampled as x_j \sim \mathcal{N}(y, \sigma^2) — i.e., every feature is a noisy version of the label, so its distribution for the two classes overlaps heavily. With enough features and a small enough training set, it’s entirely possible that pure chance makes one particular feature perfectly linearly separable on the training data alone. The model can then achieve zero training loss by placing all of its weight on that one lucky feature and ignoring every other — a classic case of over-reliance on a feature that is no more reliable than any other.
The same failure mode shows up in deep networks: with many learned features and a limited training set, some feature may become accidentally separable, and the model over-invests in it. Both regularizers below attack exactly this over-reliance.


L2 Regularization (Weight Decay)
To discourage any single weight from growing too large, add the squared L2 norm of the weights (for a matrix, the squared Frobenius norm \lVert W \rVert_F^2 = \sum_{i,j} W_{ij}^2) to the loss, scaled by a hyperparameter \lambda:
\mathcal{L}_{\text{reg}} = \mathcal{L} + \lambda \lVert W \rVert_F^2
The gradient descent update on this regularized loss is
W \leftarrow W - \eta \nabla_W\!\left(\mathcal{L} + \lambda \lVert W \rVert_F^2\right) = (1 - 2\eta\lambda)\, W - \eta \nabla_W \mathcal{L}
Since \eta and \lambda are both small, (1-2\eta\lambda) is a number just under 1 — every update multiplicatively shrinks W a little, in addition to the usual gradient step. This is why L2 regularization is also called weight decay.


Dropout
The second common regularizer, dropout (Srivastava et al. 2014) (invented at the University of Toronto), attacks over-reliance more directly: during training, each feature is independently zeroed out with probability p (a hyperparameter), and otherwise rescaled by \frac{1}{1-p}:
x_i' = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{with probability } p \\[4pt] \dfrac{x_i}{1-p} & \text{with probability } 1-p \end{cases}
The rescaling is chosen precisely so that \mathbb{E}[x_i'] = x_i — dropout doesn’t change what the network computes on average, but because any given feature might vanish on any given training step, the model can never afford to rely on just one. At test time, dropout is turned off: no features are zeroed and no rescaling is applied. Weight decay and dropout are, in practice, the two regularizers you will reach for most often in deep learning.

title: Lecture 3: Under/overfitting, Regularization, Numerical Stability, Autodiff
text:
Summary






Note



Key takeaways from Lecture 3

A training step (forward + backward) costs about 3× a forward pass: \sim|\theta| for the forward pass, and \sim2|\theta| more for the backward pass (a matrix–vector product plus an outer product per layer).
A sigmoid network’s backward recursion repeatedly multiplies by (a) the sigmoid derivative (max \tfrac14) and (b) the weight matrix transpose — the first reliably vanishes, the second can vanish or explode depending on its eigenvalues.
Xavier/Glorot initialization (\sigma = \sqrt{2/(n_{in}+n_{out})}) keeps activation and gradient variance \approx 1 at every layer, avoiding vanishing/exploding gradients from the start of training. He initialization is the ReLU-specific variant.
Automatic differentiation decomposes any model into elementary operations with known local derivatives, records them in a computational graph during the forward pass, and computes every gradient by traversing that graph backward — no hand-derived backward pass required.
Overfitting happens when a model over-relies on a feature that is accidentally informative on the training set alone. Weight decay (+\lambda\lVert W\rVert_F^2, i.e. shrink weights every step) and dropout (randomly zero features during training) both discourage this over-reliance.

title: Lecture 4: Gradient Descent, Adaptive Gradient Methods
text:
Gradient Descent
Overview. So far in this course we have used gradient descent to optimize our models without saying much about why it works. This lecture takes a closer look. We first justify the gradient descent update through a first-order Taylor expansion, which also explains the central role of the learning rate. We then move from optimizing the full training loss (batch gradient descent) to optimizing one example or a small mini-batch at a time (stochastic gradient descent), and we examine the consequences: noisier progress, the option of a learning rate schedule, and a trade-off between efficiency, noise, and parallelism. Finally, we motivate and define adaptive gradient methods, which give each parameter its own effective learning rate based on the history of its gradients. We build up to Adam, the optimizer used to train most modern neural networks.
Before returning to machine learning, it helps to set neural networks aside and consider the more general problem of minimizing a function. Call the function f(x). To minimize f means to find values of x that make f as small as possible. In machine learning the function we minimize is usually the loss and the variable we adjust is usually the model’s parameters, but for the moment we keep things generic.

title: Lecture 4: Gradient Descent, Adaptive Gradient Methods
text:
Why gradient descent works
To justify the gradient descent update, we start from a Taylor expansion of f. Writing it in one particular form, if f is infinitely differentiable and real analytic then its value at a point offset by h from x can be written as an infinite sum,
f(x + h) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{h^n f^{(n)}(x)}{n!},
where f^{(n)} is the nth derivative of f. This decomposes the function’s behavior near x into contributions from its successive derivatives. If this specific form is unfamiliar, it is the same Taylor expansion seen elsewhere, just written as a single sum.
Now set the offset to \epsilon, a placeholder for a small number, and expand. The n=0 term is \epsilon^0 f(x)/0! = f(x). The n=1 term is \epsilon^1 f'(x)/1! = \epsilon f'(x). Every remaining term carries a factor of \epsilon^2 or higher; because \epsilon is small and we divide by n!, these terms are dominated by \epsilon^2, which is small. Collecting them into an error term,
f(x + \epsilon) = f(x) + \epsilon f'(x) + \mathcal{O}(\epsilon^2).
What this says is that, as long as we stay close enough to x, a good approximation of f is a linear one: f(x) is the value at the point, f'(x) is the slope of the tangent line there, and \epsilon f'(x) moves us along that tangent line. We would not expect a tangent line to approximate an arbitrary function well everywhere, but for small enough \epsilon it is a good local approximation.
Now comes the step that produces something familiar. Set \epsilon = -\eta f'(x). We can treat this as small as long as the learning rate \eta is small and the function is reasonably smooth, so that f'(x) is not too large. Substituting into the first-order expansion,
f\big(x - \eta f'(x)\big) = f(x) - \eta \big(f'(x)\big)^2 + \mathcal{O}\!\big(\eta^2 (f'(x))^2\big).
The middle term on the right is subtracted and is non-negative: \eta is positive and (f'(x))^2 is a square, so even when f'(x) is negative the product is positive. Provided the error term is small enough to ignore, moving from x to x - \eta f'(x) therefore decreases f:

f\big(x - \eta f'(x)\big) \;\lesssim\; f(x) \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x \leftarrow x - \eta f'(x).

The \lesssim is approximate precisely because of the discarded error term. As long as that error is small, we can be reasonably confident the new value of x produces a smaller f, which is exactly what minimization requires. Repeating the update drives f steadily downward. Geometrically, we stand at x, follow the tangent line a small distance downhill to x - \eta f'(x), and the gap between the function and the tangent line is the error we are neglecting.
We will return to the question of what happens when that error is not small.


The learning rate
The size of the error term, and therefore whether the update actually decreases f, depends on the learning rate \eta. This gives three qualitatively different regimes.
If we want to be sure the approximate inequality holds, we can make \epsilon = -\eta f'(x) very small by making \eta very small. This works, but each step then covers very little ground, so minimizing the function takes a great many iterations. In deep learning each iteration means a forward and backward pass through the model, and, as we saw last lecture (Lecture 3), adding the backward pass roughly triples the cost of the forward pass alone. A very small learning rate multiplies an already expensive computation by the number of steps, and training may run out of time or budget before it converges.
The opposite choice is a large \eta, to make faster progress. But when \eta is too large the error term is no longer negligible, and the update can overshoot so badly that the new point is worse than where it started. Instead of decreasing, f increases, and increases again on the next step. This is divergence: when training a model, we see the loss climbing rather than falling.
The learning rate we want is somewhere between these, “just right”: large enough to make steady progress, small enough not to diverge. In general the right value is hard to characterize in advance, because we do not have access to the function’s curvature ahead of time and every problem differs. In practice we tune \eta as a hyperparameter, adjusting it until we observe consistent, reasonably rapid decrease in the loss.


  
  Choosing the learning rate η
  
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    small η
    slow: many tiny steps

The multivariate case
The same derivation carries over to functions of many variables, which is the case that matters for us since models have many parameters. For a scalar-valued function of a vector \bm{x}, the gradient is the vector of partial derivatives,
\nabla_{\bm{x}} f(\bm{x}) = \left[\frac{\partial f(\bm{x})}{\partial x_1},\; \frac{\partial f(\bm{x})}{\partial x_2},\; \dots\right]^\top,
each entry taken with respect to one component of \bm{x}. The first-order Taylor expansion now uses a vector offset \bm{\epsilon} with small norm,
f(\bm{x} + \bm{\epsilon}) = f(\bm{x}) + \bm{\epsilon}^\top \nabla_{\bm{x}} f(\bm{x}) + \mathcal{O}\big(\|\bm{\epsilon}\|^2\big).
Setting \bm{\epsilon} = -\eta\, \nabla_{\bm{x}} f(\bm{x}) with a single scalar learning rate \eta > 0,
f\big(\bm{x} - \eta \nabla_{\bm{x}} f(\bm{x})\big) = f(\bm{x}) - \eta\, \nabla_{\bm{x}} f(\bm{x})^\top \nabla_{\bm{x}} f(\bm{x}) + \mathcal{O}(\cdots) \;\lesssim\; f(\bm{x}).
The subtracted term is again non-negative, since it is the inner product of a vector with itself scaled by a positive \eta. The idea is identical to the single-variable case. It is worth noting that \eta remains a single scalar: we do not use a different learning rate for each component of \bm{x}. The implications of that choice will occupy the second half of this lecture.

section: From Batch to Stochastic Gradient Descent
text:
From Batch to Stochastic Gradient Descent
Returning to machine learning, the function we minimize is the loss. For a single training example the loss depends on an input, a target, and the parameters. Using the (i) superscript to index the ith example of the training set, we write
\mathcal{L}\big(\bm{y}^{(i)}, \bm{x}^{(i)}, \bm{\theta}\big) = \mathcal{L}_i(\bm{\theta}).
The abbreviation \mathcal{L}_i(\bm{\theta}) reflects that, although the loss takes three arguments, the one we differentiate with respect to is \bm{\theta}; for a fixed example the input and target are constants. We will return shortly to the fact that \mathcal{L}_i is a different function for each example.
We want to minimize the loss across the whole training set by changing \bm{\theta}. Define the full training loss as the average of the per-example losses over a training set of size N,
\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathcal{L}_i(\bm{\theta}).
By linearity of the gradient, the gradient of the average is the average of the gradients,
\nabla_{\bm{\theta}} \mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \nabla_{\bm{\theta}} \mathcal{L}_i(\bm{\theta}),
so each gradient descent step uses the average gradient over the entire dataset:
\bm{\theta} \leftarrow \bm{\theta} - \eta\, \nabla_{\bm{\theta}} \mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}).
This is batch gradient descent — “batch” here meaning the full dataset, not a mini-batch in the sense the word usually carries today.

Stochastic gradient descent
Batch gradient descent is not what we have actually been doing in this course. Instead, in the most extreme case, we compute each update from the gradient of a single per-example loss, where the example is drawn uniformly at random,
\bm{\theta} \leftarrow \bm{\theta} - \eta\, \nabla_{\bm{\theta}} \mathcal{L}_i(\bm{\theta}), \qquad i \sim \operatorname{Uniform}\{1, \dots, N\}.
We might feel comfortable with this because in expectation the single-example update matches the batch update. Since each index has probability 1/N,
\mathbb{E}\big[\nabla_{\bm{\theta}} \mathcal{L}_i(\bm{\theta})\big] = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{j=1}^{N} \nabla_{\bm{\theta}} \mathcal{L}_j(\bm{\theta}) = \nabla_{\bm{\theta}} \mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}).

Definition. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) updates the parameters using the gradient of the loss on a single randomly drawn example. In expectation this update equals the full-batch update, but any individual update uses only one example. In common usage “SGD” usually refers to the mini-batch version introduced below rather than this single-example form.

There is an important distinction hiding behind the notation. As i changes, \mathcal{L}_i is not merely evaluated at a different point — it is a different function. The loss encodes how changing the parameters changes the loss for a particular input–target pair, and changing the pair changes that relationship. If we were to minimize \mathcal{L}_i for a single fixed i, we would drive the loss on that one example toward zero, potentially overfitting it, with no expectation that the minimizer of one example’s loss is the minimizer of another’s.


SGD optimizes a different function each iteration
This is worth picturing. When we justified gradient descent at the start of the lecture, we assumed f was a single, fixed function. In SGD we instead draw a different function from a pool at every iteration. If we plot the loss against the parameters, the full-batch loss \mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}) is one curve, while the per-example losses \mathcal{L}_i(\bm{\theta}) scatter around it — each pointing us in a somewhat different direction.

At each iteration we descend a different one of these per-example curves. The direction that decreases the sampled \mathcal{L}_i need not decrease another, so successive steps can partly work against one another. Far from a minimum this tends not to matter: the per-example losses mostly agree on the direction to move. Near a minimum, though, they increasingly disagree, and rather than settling, the parameters bounce around. The training loss reflects this — it falls reliably at first and then grows noisy and plateaus as we approach the minimum, because the function being sampled changes from step to step.


Learning rate schedules
One widespread response to this stalling is a learning rate schedule: rather than holding \eta fixed, use a different value \eta(t) at each iteration t. Several common choices are

\begin{aligned}
\eta(t) &= \eta \quad \text{(constant)}, \\
\eta(t) &= \eta_i \;\text{ if } t_i \le t < t_{i+1} \quad \text{(piecewise constant)}, \\
\eta(t) &= \eta_0\, e^{-\lambda t} \quad \text{(exponential)}.
\end{aligned}

The constant schedule is what we have used so far. A piecewise-constant schedule holds the learning rate at a sensible value for most of training and then drops it in the late phase, when SGD’s progress would otherwise stall, so that smaller steps can make further progress; the intervals t_i and rates \eta_i are hyperparameters. A common variant is to not fix the intervals in advance but instead drop the rate — say by a factor of ten — whenever progress stalls, an adaptive rather than predefined schedule. The exponential schedule decays the rate continuously at a speed set by \lambda. Another popular choice, which we will not write out, is the cosine schedule, which decays the rate from its initial value to near zero over a fixed training duration T following the shape of a cosine curve. The shared intuition is that early in training the per-example losses agree and a larger rate is safe, while later a smaller rate makes less noisy progress toward the minimum.


Mini-batch SGD
The other main response, and the one used in practice, is to sample not a single example but a mini-batch of B examples at each iteration and use their average gradient,

\bm{\theta} \leftarrow \bm{\theta} - \eta\, \frac{1}{B} \sum_{i=1}^{B} \nabla_{\bm{\theta}} \mathcal{L}_i(\bm{\theta}).

This looks like the batch update but averages over B randomly sampled examples rather than all N. This is mini-batch stochastic gradient descent, and it is what “SGD” usually means in practice. To see why an intermediate B is attractive, it helps to note three properties.
SGD can be more efficient than batch gradient descent. Imagine a training set built by duplicating a single example N times. Every per-example gradient would be identical, so batch gradient descent would compute the same expensive gradient N times, average them, and arrive at exactly what one computation would have given. More generally, when the per-example gradient \nabla_{\bm{\theta}} \mathcal{L}_i is generally aligned with the full-batch gradient \nabla_{\bm{\theta}} \mathcal{L} — that is, when a single example or a small batch approximates the full-batch update well — we get essentially the same update for much less work. When the dataset carries a lot of redundancy this is the case, and in practice it often is.
SGD can be noisy. Because the sampled loss, and therefore the update, changes at every iteration, progress is less reliable than with the full-batch gradient, as the previous figure showed.
SGD is less parallelizable. Suppose we had N accelerators. Batch gradient descent could compute all N per-example gradients at once, so a full step would take about as long as a single gradient. SGD cannot do this: the update at iteration t depends on the parameters produced at iteration t-1, so its steps are inherently serial.
Taken together, these explain why mini-batch SGD is the standard choice. Batch gradient descent wastes computation on redundant data; pure single-example SGD is noisy and serial. A mini-batch size B offers a middle ground — reasonably reliable gradients, some parallelism across the B examples, and far less wasted work than the full batch.
